extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, and journalism students (media scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical considerations reporters and editors use when choosing and using sources during story selection and production for news media. Emphasizes constraints of deadlines, medium (TV vs print), and reporter role (beat vs general).

rubrics_metrics.name: Past suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: If sources have provided information leading to suitable stories in the past, they are apt to be chosen again, until they eventually become regular sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular sources may become repetitious and be 'banished' (e.g., Newsweek hung a map to banish overused sources, normal term one year). Story selectors prefer familiar sources early in story selection because they can be evaluated quickly; beware boredom and repetition from single-purpose organizations or perennial experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources are judged by their ability to supply a lot of information without undue expenditure of staff time and effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer spokespeople and public officials who can speak for an agency (reduces need for many interviews). Use central clearing houses to quickly supply names. Production constraints explain emphasis on government plans/new policies (one official yields the story) and the predominance of high officials in the news. Example: relying on alumni offices produced a biased sample, prompting further interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Story selectors want reliable sources whose information requires the least amount of checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story or fact is controversial or not readily believed, reporters are expected to gather proof from at least two separate and independent sources. When reporters can explicitly attribute information to a source, they often consider their responsibility fulfilled (the audience must judge credibility) — 'we don't deal in facts but in attributed opinions.' Nevertheless, an unreliable source can damage journalistic credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: When reliability cannot be checked quickly enough, story selectors look for trustworthy sources: those who do not limit themselves to self-serving information, try to be accurate, and, above all, are honest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists keep records of sources' honesty and warn colleagues about liars. Indicators of trustworthiness include cooperation, cordiality, willingness to explain inconsistencies, formal authority, and social proximity/similarity. Journalists are generally distrustful of politicians and more trusting of peers, friends, and socially proximate sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: All other things being equal, journalists prefer to resort to sources in official positions of authority and responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoritative sources are assumed less likely to lie openly and are more persuasive because their facts/opinions are official. Using authoritative sources helps reporters defend their coverage to editors/executives and makes stories easier to sell to story selectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview sources must be able to make their point concisely and, preferably, dramatically; television favors speakers using standard (national middle-class) English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television interviewees are often rehearsed and 'fed' questions off-camera; magazines may edit quotes ('helping the quoted guy') to achieve concision and standard English. Sources with poor grammar or convoluted syntax may be edited; preference for standard English can bias selection toward certain social groups and institutions ('the best schools give us the best interviews').

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistics and availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical/logistical factors can make otherwise suitable sources unusable: people out of town, limited camera crews, broken equipment, film problems, and transit delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production deadlines and scarce resources (especially for television and networks) mean stories can be lost because sources or equipment are unavailable. These difficulties are rarely publicized but drive post-mortem reorganizations and staffing changes when recurring. Networks typically suffer more from such problems than magazines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data limitation (minimizing sources/information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors intentionally limit the number of sources and the volume of information they gather to fit time/space constraints and processing ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters try to obtain the most suitable news from the fewest sources quickly and cheaply. Producers and editors discourage unnecessary footage/files. General reporters especially must practice data limitation because they come to assignments with limited angles and little time to process conflicting information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbiotic relationships and co-optation (cost–benefit of upsetting sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beat reporters develop close, sometimes symbiotic relationships with sources; this closeness facilitates inside stories but can lead to self-censorship, co-optation, or agency influence on reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters must weigh costs and benefits of displeasing sources (risk losing future access vs. publishing a scoop). Agencies may pressure reporters (e.g., banishing or withholding access for noncompliant reporters). Rotations of reporters (war/White House correspondents) and occasional reliance on non-beat columnists fill gaps left by self-censorship. Examples: Pentagon withholding information; White House privileges tempt reporters; reporters who appear co-opted lose peer/superior confidence and may be moved off a beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter role: beat reporters vs general reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporter type shapes source selection and use: beat reporters (locational or substantive) become participant-observers with deep source ties; general reporters are outsiders with little prior knowledge and different practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beat reporters develop rapport, inside information, and may be constrained by obligations to sources; substantive beats produce specialists who nonetheless must serve lay audiences. General reporters lack deep contacts, rely on authoritative sources, can ask more provocative questions, and focus on dramatic/highlight aspects of a story. Assignments, rehearsal, access to background materials, and expectations differ across these roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer cross-checking (fraternization/herd instinct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters reduce uncertainty by exchanging observations and impressions with other reporters; this practice legitimates counts and conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When observing or reporting under uncertainty, journalists compare notes with peers (e.g., crowd estimates at demonstrations) and swap impressions about source trustworthiness. This 'herd instinct' can reassure editors about a story's credibility, but it also represents a collective validation practice rather than independent verification.
